title: Closed-Loop Position Control System
short_description: A PID-controlled cart-on-rails system using an Arduino, ultrasonic sensor and servo motor, achieving stable position control with under 2mm steady-state error.
full_description: A closed-loop position control system built to balance a cart on a pair of rails, using an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor to measure position and a servo motor to adjust rail angle. The controller was designed in Simulink and deployed to an Arduino, with the full pipeline — sensor calibration, plant modelling, filtering and PID tuning — built and validated first in simulation, then on physical hardware.
motivation: The brief was to design and build a small-scale closed-loop position control system from first principles: derive the plant dynamics, design a controller against that model, then validate the whole pipeline on physical hardware rather than in simulation alone.
methodology: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor was calibrated against known reference positions to find its gain and offset, and the servo-to-rail-angle relationship was calibrated separately. A first-order IIR low-pass filter (20Hz cutoff, against a 100Hz Nyquist limit) was designed to attenuate sensor noise. The system's plant transfer function was derived from a free-body diagram of the cart on the rail using Newton's second law with small-angle approximation, and a PID controller was designed and tuned in simulation before being deployed to the physical rig via Simulink and an Arduino Uno.
results: Simulated PID gains of Kp = 5.42, Ki = 0.87, Kd = 0.61 required substantial re-tuning for the physical system — down to Kp = 3.41, Ki = 0.53, Kd = 0.24 — to avoid oscillation once real-world friction and air resistance were accounted for. The IIR filter reduced measurement noise by over 80%, and the system achieved stable closed-loop position control with under 2mm steady-state error, though a small residual steady-state error remained due to the limits of the integral term against unmodelled disturbances.
lessons_learned: The gap between the simulated and physical system was the main lesson: friction, air resistance and structural vibration all introduced damping and disturbances the model didn't capture, and closing that gap took more re-tuning than the initial design. Future improvements identified include a zero-phase (bidirectional) filter to remove the phase lag introduced by the IIR filter, and physically lowering the rig's centre of mass to reduce vibration.
